passage.title: Why Every Town Needs Its Market
paras: Before the supermarkets open their sliding doors, before the first delivery van has finished its rounds, there is a place in your town that is already awake. Listen: crates landing on trestles, a stallholder singing (not well), the first regulars arriving because they know the best goes early.

Markets are not simply places to buy cheap fruit. For a hundred and fifty years and more, they have been where a town looks after its own: where a seller saves soft tomatoes for a customer who cannot chew, where bruised fruit is let go for a few pence at closing time, where kindness passes across a counter as easily as change.

passage.title: The Last Stall
paras: At four o'clock the market began to fold itself away. Awnings sagged, tables shrank into their legs, and the cobbles, freed at last, shone with puddles and lost grapes. Only one stall stayed open: a narrow table, a single crate, and an old man who seemed to be waiting for someone who was late.
